activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: A blending stump, or tortillon, is a tightly rolled paper stick used to smooth pencil shading into gradual tones without using your finger.
story:
Jace had drawn the same circle nine times, and it still looked like a fried egg. He pressed his pencil down the right side of the sphere, trying to make the shadow darker where the lamp sat, but the tones came out in stripes instead of a smooth slide from light to dark. Across the art room, Lambert held up his own drawing, which looked so round you could have bounced it off the floor.

"Yours looks like an onion," said Yousif, squinting at Jace's paper. "A sad onion."

"It's supposed to look like a planet," Jace said. "With a light source." He pointed at the desk lamp Ms. Carvalho had set on the front table. "See, the highlight goes there, where the light hits it, and the shadow goes on the far side, and the cast shadow falls on the table over here." He knew all that. He'd written it in his sketchbook. Knowing it and drawing it were two entirely different adversaries.

Yousif, working beside him, rubbed his thumb hard across his sphere to soften the stripes. The graphite smeared all right, but it also went blotchy, and a greasy shine appeared where his finger had been. He held the paper up to the lamp and groaned. "Mine looks like it's been handled by a ham sandwich."

Ms. Carvalho passed behind them on her way to the supply cabinet. Without a lecture, without even stopping long, she set a thin paper stick on Yousif's table. "Try that instead of your finger," she said. "It's called a blending stump. Some people call it a tortillon." Then she moved on to argue with Lambert about whether his sphere needed more cast shadow.

Jace picked it up first. It was tightly rolled gray paper, pointed at one end, soft as a pencil made of felt. He touched it to the dark edge of his sphere and swept it in small circles, and the stripes melted into each other, one gray breathing into the next, like fog rolling downhill. He worked the stump over the highlight less, over the shadow more, calibrating the pressure until the sphere began to bulge off the page. It wasn't arbitrary anymore, the way shading had felt for nine failed planets. The light had a direction, and the stump followed it.

Yousif leaned over. "Okay. That's actually annoying how good that is."

"You can have it when I'm done." Jace spun the stump between his fingers, then went back to the cast shadow, dragging the darkest tone out from under the sphere's bottom edge, where no light could reach. He thought about last year, when he'd quit the drawing club after one bad afternoon because a picture of a horse had turned out looking like a park bench. He'd told himself he just wasn't the kind of person who could do this. Now he wasn't so sure that was ever a real kind of thing to be.

"Done," Yousif announced, holding up his own sphere, still a little greasy in one corner but round as a marble.

Jace signed his name small in the corner of his planet, then held the paper at arm's length toward the lamp.

"Almost bounces," he said.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
The silence between desks had lasted three days, and Florence decided to investigate it like any other mystery. Krystal, her best friend since second grade, sat two rows over and would not look at her, all because Florence had forgotten to nominate Krystal for the class garden committee and had nominated Fanny instead. The air between them felt brittle, like a cookie left out too long. Florence wondered: was the silence about the committee, or about something older underneath it?

She tried an experiment. At lunch she left a note on Krystal's desk that said, "I forgive you for the silent treatment. Do you forgive me?" She watched from the doorway, heart pounding with suspense, as Krystal read it, crumpled it, and dropped it in the recycling bin. Hmm, Florence thought. So forgiving had not fixed anything. Interesting.

After school she found Ms. Farah-Ali watering the spider plant by the window. Florence explained the crumpled note. "I said I forgave her and nothing happened. Does forgiveness not work?"

Ms. Farah-Ali tilted the watering can. "Did you know my sister studies this? She says forgiving means letting go of resentment, and reconciling means rebuilding the relationship." She set the can down. "Two different jobs."

Florence stood very still. Two different jobs. She had done one and expected the other. She had let go of her mad feelings, sure, but the friendship itself still had a hole in it, and nobody was building anything.

So she tried the second job. The next morning she carried two seed packets, marigold and zinnia, and set them on Krystal's desk. "For the garden committee," she whispered. "You know more about dirt than anyone. Fanny nominated you for the flower team, actually. I just forgot to tell you." Krystal stared at the packets, then at her. "You're forgiven," Krystal said slowly. "But you have to help me carry the watering bucket all week." Florence grinned and shook her hand across the aisle.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The class discussion had started with the spring festival, because the festival committee had made two hundred dollars in revenue last year and Ms. Walker wanted ideas for spending it. Then Presley said the money should fund a heritage booth, and Abrielle said she wanted to run it, and Presley said no.

"You're not really from the community," Presley said. "Your grandma moved here before your mom was even born."

"That doesn't decide it," Abrielle said. "I decide it."

Around the room, people took sides. Jade wrote both arguments at the top of her notebook page, trying to keep her notes objective, but the argument kept sliding into opinion, so she underlined the actual question instead: who gets to decide which group a person belongs to? That was the hidden thing. The booth and the money and the grandma were only the surface, and she could not answer the surface question until she answered the one underneath.

She raised her hand. "Ms. Walker, is there an actual rule about this, or just opinions?"

Ms. Walker told her to find out, so Jade took the classroom laptop and searched while the others argued on. It took three tries. Then she found it: the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007. Article 33, near the top of the page, said Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.

Jade stood up. "The United Nations says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership. Adopted 13 September 2007. So it's not Presley's call."

Presley folded her arms. "So who runs the booth?"

"Whoever the community says is part of it," Jade said, "and Abrielle can ask them herself."

Abrielle pulled the laptop closer and began scrolling, her finger stopping on each line.

"Send me that link," she said.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service in the United States.
story:
Victoria found the permission slip on the kitchen table on Saturday morning, half covered by a grocery receipt. Her mom had written "sign this" across the top. It said the whole class was signed up to volunteer at the community food bank on the Monday holiday in January, and it mentioned something called the King Holiday and Service Act.

On Monday she stood beside Atlas in the food bank warehouse, sorting cans of beans into crates. The air smelled like cardboard and cold metal, and the concrete floor hummed under a running freezer. Atlas kept checking a sheet of paper in his pocket.

"Why are we even here on a holiday?" Victoria asked. "Shouldn't we be off school?"

"We are off school," Atlas said. He pulled out the paper. "This is my volunteer log. I need ten hours for extra credit in Mr. Bondarenko's class, and today counts for four." He smoothed the log flat on a crate, like it might wrinkle and stop counting.

Victoria stacked three cans and thought about the permission slip. Her mom usually worked on Mondays, and so did half the neighborhood, so it wasn't just a convenient day. She counted the other volunteers: a family at the bread table, two women stocking shelves, a man her dad's age lifting rice sacks. It looked like everybody had chosen this day on purpose.

At the break, Mr. Bondarenko handed out juice boxes from a cooler, since the food bank budget couldn't cover the expense of drinks for thirty students. Victoria asked him why the day had a special name on the slip.

"The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994," he said. "It made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service."

"Wait, so that's why we're off school," Victoria said. "So we can do this."

"That was the idea," he said, and moved on to the next cooler.

After the break, a woman from the front desk pinned a chart to the wall showing which food boxes had gone out that morning. Some donors had given under the label anonymous, and the chart showed those boxes marked the same as the named ones. Victoria noticed the anonymous boxes went to the same families as everything else, no different shelf, no different line. She decided she would rather be on the chart than off it, and she said so.

"Good," said the woman at the desk. "Because the tape gun just broke and I need someone who'll persist through about forty more boxes."

Victoria picked up the spare tape roll and pulled a long strip free with her teeth.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
The chat lit up at 7:42 p.m., right after the girls' basketball game. Deanna had sent a screenshot of the league stat page, and beneath it a single trophy emoji. Arianne had taken one shot all season, made it, and now her name sat at the top of the shooting percentage list with a perfect 100 beside it. "Best shooter in the league," Deanna typed, "and she'll emphasize it in gym class tomorrow, just watch."

Landon stared at his phone on the diagonal shelf above his desk where he propped it while doing homework. Something about that 100 bothered him, but he couldn't say what. He scrolled down the list. His cousin's name was near the bottom, at 48 percent, with sixty-two shots taken. Sixty-two! Landon tapped out a message, deleted it, tapped out another, deleted that too. His conscience nudged him: Arianne was in this chat, silent tonight, probably reading every word.

Then he saw it. One shot. One make. Landon pulled up the stat page himself and checked every column twice, scrolling slowly so he wouldn't miss anything. Arianne had attempted exactly one basket the entire season. A player who made one shot out of one attempt would shoot 100 percent, even if she never touched the ball again. His cousin had made thirty shots out of sixty-two and looked worse on the list.

Landon typed: "Arianne took one shot all season. One. Anyone makes that one, they're at 100." He held his thumb over send. In the game thread, Deanna was already posting "QUEEN OF THE COURT."

He sent it.

For a full minute, nobody replied. The typing bubble appeared, vanished, appeared again. Then Arianne's name popped up with a message he hadn't expected: "Thanks. Coach keeps saying I need to take more shots. I've been scared to ruin it."

"So ruin it," Landon typed. "Take sixty. Then the number means something."

Arianne replied with a single emoji of a player taking a jump shot.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Deodorants do not stop sweat; they fight odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance.
story:
Antoine sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office, holding his elbow where he'd banged it in gym class, but that was not what he was thinking about. He was thinking about the transparent bottle of deodorant spray in his backpack, and about how Journey had announced to half the locker room that Antoine's shirt was soaked anyway, so what was the point?

The nurse called him back, and while the doctor examined his elbow, Antoine stared at the wall. Three weeks ago he had started using the spray every morning, exactly like the label said. Three weeks ago the damp spots on his shirts had started showing up too, and he had assumed the spray was broken. His dad had offered to buy a different brand, but Antoine had wanted to figure out the problem himself, mostly because the drugstore cashier already knew him by name and it was getting embarrassing.

"Something else bothering you?" the doctor asked, following his stare.

"It's my deodorant. It doesn't work. I still sweat right through it." Antoine hesitated, then plunged ahead. "Am I... broken? Is something wrong with me? Do I have an infection or something?"

The doctor chuckled. "No infection. You're eleven. Sweat is part of growing up; everyone gets it." He paused. "Deodorant was never meant to stop sweat. It fights odor. It slows down the bacteria on your skin, the ones that make the smell, and covers what's left with fragrance."

Antoine sat very still. Bacteria. Living things on his skin, too small to see, making the smell. The deodorant hindered them, like a crowd of tiny troublemakers being held back at a gate, and meanwhile the sweat just kept flowing right past. Two different problems. He had been fighting one and blaming the other.

"So the damp is normal," he said slowly, "and the smell is the part the spray handles."

"Exactly. Daily shower, deodorant, and a clean shirt, and you'll be fine."

Walking out, Antoine pulled out his phone and texted Journey: it's not broken, bacteria make the smell and the spray only fights them. Then he added, gym in ten minutes, and if you say one word about my shirt, I'm telling everyone about your screaming during the flu shot.

Journey's reply buzzed back before he even reached the door: "ONE WORD? THAT WAS A FULL PARAGRAPH."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
story:
Hailey slid into the seat by the window in the school library and opened the laptop Mr. Shapiro had signed out to her. On the screen was her German assignment: five full sentences describing her family and her pets. She had written the first one the night before, and this morning the library computer's spell-checker had gone wild.

Every word for a thing was underlined in red. Hund. Katze. Schwester. Bruder. Even Schule, in the sentence about her older brother. At first she assumed the checker simply didn't know German, but then she noticed something odd. Ich, habe, und, and meine were all left alone. Only the nouns were flagged.

Miley leaned over from the next computer. "What's wrong with yours?"

"Look at this," Hailey whispered. "Every single thing-word is marked wrong. But the other words aren't. That's not random." She had a theory forming, and she wanted to test it before she believed it. She typed the sentence again, this time making each noun a capital: Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze. The red lines vanished, one by one, like puddles drying up. She sat back so fast her chair squeaked.

"That can't be a coincidence," Miley said.

"It isn't. Watch, I'll refute my own idea before I trust it." Hailey typed her next sentence with a lowercase noun buried in the middle. The red squiggle came back instantly, under exactly that word. She deleted the lowercase version and wrote it correctly: Meine Mutter gibt Impfungen in einer Klinik. "My mom's a nurse," she explained. "Flu vaccine, everything. So that sentence is actually true."

From across the room, Meghan raised a defiant fist at her own screen. "Mine's still all red and I refuse to fix forty words!"

"Capitalize the nouns," Hailey called softly. "Every noun. All of them, even in the middle of a sentence." Meghan started typing, and Hailey watched the squiggles disappear down Meghan's screen, row after row.

Mr. Shapiro looked up from his desk. "Hailey, how's it going over there?"

She grinned and turned the laptop toward him. "See for yourself."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290.
story:
Rose sat in the waiting room of the optometrist's office squinting at a poster of an eye chart, which was pointless, since the whole reason she was here was that she could not read anything smaller than a stop sign. Her friend Rhys had come along because his mother was picking them both up for soccer, and he was now reading every frame on the wall out loud in a dramatic announcer voice. "Rose. Rose. Ladies and gentlemen, she cannot see her own shoelaces."

"I can too," Rose said, holding up a sneaker. "I just can't tell if they're tied."

The door chimed and Jay walked in with a parent, waved, and plopped into the chair beside Rhys, immediately grabbing the sample frames. Jay put on a pair with lenses thick as hockey pucks. "Behold. I am an impulsive organism of the year 1290, and I have invented spectacles."

Rose blinked. "Where did you get 1290?"

Jay lowered the glasses. "Mr. Liu told us last week. The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290. I wrote it on my hand because it sounded cool, then sweated half of it off." The ink was indeed smudged, but the numbers survived.

Rose leaned back, thinking. If glasses were only invented around then, that meant for all of history before 1290, everyone who couldn't see well just... couldn't see well. She tried to imagine monks copying books with their noses touching the page. No wonder, she thought, some of those old manuscripts looked like they were written by someone doing it blindfolded. She turned the idea over, testing it. "So if someone in, say, 1200 was nearsighted, they'd have to hold a book really close, or get someone else to read it."

"Or squint," said Rhys, squinting at her to demonstrate. "Like you. You're basically medieval."

"You're basically a medieval sandwich," Rose said, but she was still working on it. It was strange to think that something invisible, a person's blurry eyesight, had been there forever, but the fix for it only showed up in one place, central Italy, around 1290. Before that, nobody had the tool, so everyone just adapted.

The optometrist called her name before she could finish the thought. Inside, he flipped lenses in a big frame and asked which was better, one or two, and when he finally set her new glasses on her nose, the room snapped into focus like someone had sharpened the whole world. She walked out and stared at Rhys.

"Your face has freckles," she announced. "Hundreds of them. This whole time."

Rhys covered his cheeks. "Put the medieval glasses away," he said. "Some things were better blurry."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Naming where a statistic came from, such as the organization that published it, lets readers check it and makes a persuasive essay more believable.
story:
Dominic slid his draft across the library table like it might bite somebody. "It's five paragraphs," he said. "Intro, three reasons, conclusion. Mr. García's rubric says so."

Melody picked it up. "You wrote that kids who eat school breakfast score higher on tests. Says who?"

"Says me. It's obvious."

Karson leaned over her shoulder. "Says who is the whole question. My cousin tried that in a debate and got demolished." He tapped the page. "Numbers need names attached."

Dominic frowned at his paper. He had three reasons why the school should serve a hot breakfast bar, and one of them was that number. He flipped through a library book about nutrition until he found a chart, then another, hunting for the source of the statistic the way Melody hunted for the last donut. He found it in a health report from a big government agency, printed the name right after the number, and watched Melody read it again.

"Now I could look it up and check," she admitted. "Which means I sort of believe you. Ugh."

"That's the trick," Dominic said. "The name is doing the persuading." He decided to elaborate, because it felt great. "It's like the number brought a permission slip."

"You are so weird," said Karson, but he copied the idea onto his own outline.

Dominic worked through the rest of the draft. He cut a sentence claiming breakfast cereal was mostly carbohydrate, because he couldn't find where that came from either, and it hurt to lose it. In his conclusion he added one more line about the agency, then read the whole thing aloud in a whisper, conducting with his pencil.

Melory clapped twice, very quietly, since they were in a library. Karson gave him a thumbs up and mouthed "says who."

Dominic grinned and mouthed back, "Says the report, that's who," and slid the finished essay into his folder before the librarian could shush them all.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
Austin's shoes had gotten small so gradually that he hadn't noticed until his toes hit the end, and now he was riding in the family car to the mall to buy new ones, size six, which felt like big news. His mom had also picked up Helen and Aiza, who were coming along to look for Halloween costumes. In the back seat, the two girls bent over a flyer.

"I'm going as a medieval peasant," Aiza announced. "The scratchy shirt, the whole thing."

"Meanwhile my sister's home being dramatic," Helen said. "She got her first period last week and she's acting like it's a royal event. She's fourteen. My cousin's sister got hers at ten, which seems really early."

Aiza shrugged. "My sister was eleven and a half. Nobody made it a royal event at our house."

Austin turned around in his seat. Fourteen, ten, eleven and a half. He did the math in his head, and the middle of those numbers landed near twelve. "Hold on," he said. "I read there was this big CDC survey, like a huge national one, and the median age for a girl's first period was about twelve. So half got it before twelve and half after."

"That's the median?" Helen said. "So my sister at fourteen isn't weird, just on the later end."

"And ten's on the early end," Aiza said. "There's a wide normal range around it."

Austin sat back, pleased with himself, then suspicious. Wait. His sample was three sisters, all from people he happened to know, which was completely biased. Three girls whose families shopped at the same mall. That couldn't prove anything. The survey, though, had asked thousands of girls all over the country, so the survey was the one to trust. His little back-seat math just happened to coincide with it, which was the best kind of luck.

At the mall, he tried on the size sixes first, and they pinched. He carried the box to the counter and called across the aisle, "Helen! Aiza! New plan. I'm a size seven now."

"Big news," Helen called back.

"The biggest," Austin said, and slid his heel into the shoe.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: Under the US Constitution, a bill becomes law without the president's signature if it is not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is still in session.
story:
Ella spread her social studies homework across Grandma's kitchen table, which smelled like coffee and toast. The assignment was to explain, in her own words, how a bill becomes a law. She had the basics down: a bill passes the House, then the Senate, and then the president signs it. But the textbook mentioned one route she could not picture at all, a route where the president did nothing.

"The quiz is Monday," she told Grandma, who was hunting through her purse for the slip of paper from the doctor so she could pick up her prescription at the pharmacy. "Can I postpone it and study Sunday instead?" Grandma said no, Monday was Monday, and left for the pharmacy.

Ella read the paragraph again. It said a bill becomes law without the president's signature if it is not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is still in session. She turned that over in her head. Ten days, but Sundays did not count, so the clock skipped right over them. And Congress had to still be in session the whole time. She tested the idea with a made-up example: a bill lands on the president's desk on a Monday, he neither signs it nor returns it, the ten days tick by without the Sundays, Congress stays in session, and the bill quietly becomes a law anyway. Doing nothing was not the same as saying no. That was the hidden part, and now she could see it.

When Douglas texted to ask what he'd missed in class, she typed back: "President can ignore a bill and it still becomes law. 10 days, skip Sundays, Congress has to still be in session. Wild, right?" He replied with a row of exclamation marks.

Grandma came home, set the pharmacy bag on the counter, and frowned at the calendar by the fridge. "Good thing you can't postpone Monday," she said. "Your grandfather's stubbornness about calendars was practically hereditary, and you have it too."

"Then I'll finish tonight," Ella said, and picked up her pencil.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, which is why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms.
story:
Brooklyn had been waiting for this field trip since September, because the Millbrook Historical Museum kept one thing she had to see: a quilt stitched in 1848 by girls her own age. The bus barely stopped before she, Leilani, and Charlotte were through the doors, following Mr. Ba past the blacksmith tools and the old schoolhouse desk. But when they reached the textile room, Brooklyn stopped. The lights were so dim she could hardly make out the quilt's faded stars. "That's it?" Leilani whispered. "I can barely see anything. Why would they hang it in the dark?"

Brolyn frowned. On the wall near the door hung a faded sampler, its embroidery so pale the thread looked like breath on glass. Beside it, a bright reproduction banner, clearly newer, sat under full lights. Why would the museum treat two pieces of cloth so differently? Then she remembered a sign near the entrance about workers who would install a new display case that afternoon; the gallery would close at two for the work. Their bus left at one thirty. Mr. Ba checked his watch and said, "Ten minutes here, then we regroup."

Charlotte pulled out her phone and snapped a flash photo of the quilt, and a guard stepped over at once, asking her to turn the flash off. That was the clue Brooklyn needed. Bright light, even for a moment, was treated like something invasive, something to be kept away from these old fabrics. Light, she reasoned, must be slowly fading the dyes and pigments in the textiles, and probably in paper and paintings too, which was why the delicate things sat in dim rooms. She tested it quietly by asking the guide at the door, "So the dark isn't to save electricity?" The guide smiled and shook her head. "No, dear. It's for the cloth."

Brooklyn looked at Leilani, still squinting and disappointed. She remembered the postcard rack in the gift shop, the one Mr. Ba had said they could visit if they finished early. "Come on," she said, tugging Leilani's sleeve. "There's a better way to see it." In the shop's bright light, Leilani found a postcard of the quilt, its colors printed rich and true, and her whole face lifted. Brooklyn paid for it with her last two dollars and slid it across. "Now you can look as long as you want." Leilani held it up next to the dark doorway and whispered, "It's a privilege, getting to see it at all."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Bulb filaments are made of tungsten because it has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
The bulb on Landon's lab table refused to light, which felt like a personal insult. He had clipped the wire to the battery, flipped the little switch twice, and even held the bulb up to the window as if sunlight might embarrass it into working. Across the table, Georges watched with the patience of someone who had already finished his own circuit and was now prioritizing gloating over helping.

"Maybe the bulb's dead," Georges offered. "Dead like your volcano project?"

"That volcano was a solid B minus," Landon said. He unscrewed the bulb and peered at the tiny wire coiled inside the glass. Beside their lab packets sat a plastic card from the museum field trip, the one with a magnified photo of a filament. Landon squinted at the small print. "Hey. It says filaments are made of tungsten because it has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius."

"Three thousand four hundred," Georges repeated, sounding it out like money. "That's like... a lot of pizza ovens."

Marika leaned over from the next table, holding her glowing bulb like a trophy. "If yours doesn't work, it's not the filament melting, trust me. Those things survive 3,400 degrees. Your battery is nine volts." Landon looked at his tangle of clips and realized he had attached both wires to the same battery terminal, which meant the electricity had nowhere to go. He had been blaming a wire that could survive being molten, when the real culprit was his own sloppy fingers.

He unclipped one wire, moved it to the other terminal, and flipped the switch. The bulb bloomed yellow, warm and smug, and Landon threw both arms up like he'd scored a goal. "Ladies and gentlemen, tungsten!"

"Can we prioritize cleanup now?" Marika said, nodding toward Mr. Nielsen, who was drifting their way with the expression of a man who had seen a hundred dead volcanoes and survived them all.

Landon grinned and flicked the switch off and on one more time, just because he could.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
story:
At 7:42 on Tuesday night, Piper's phone buzzed so many times it nearly slid off her desk. The group chat, Room 12 Rocket Scientists, was being invaded by Alix, who had typed one message after another about a science article she'd found: a study where some kids got a new allergy medicine and others got the old one. "And guess what," Alix wrote, "the kids didn't even get to PICK. Some lab person just put them in groups. Rude, right?"

Eloi replied with a shrugging emoji. "If I volunteered for that, I'd pick the new medicine. It's new. Obviously."

Piper stared at the screen. Her little brother took allergy medicine every morning, and it only sort of worked, so she wanted the new one to be real. But something about the picking bothered her, like a loose tooth she couldn't stop probing. She typed, "What if everyone who picked the new one was different somehow? Like older? Or healthier?" Then she deleted it, because that was a guess, not a test.

She grabbed a notebook. In the margin she wrote her idea like a scientist would: maybe when people choose their own group, the groups aren't alike. To check it, she needed data. At school the next morning she asked Mr. Cheung if she could borrow five minutes of homeroom. "For science," she said. He raised an eyebrow but nodded.

She wrote two options on the board. Option A: a new sport where you might get to be team captain. Option B: a regular sport, no captain, but free snacks. "Pick one," she told the class. "Don't say it out loud. Write it down." Twenty-six slips of paper landed in the box, and Piper, who was meticulous about counting, tallied them twice at lunch. Option A got eleven votes. Option B got fifteen. Then she flipped the slips over and matched handwriting to the seating chart, and her stomach did a small flip. Almost every kid who picked captain was a sixth grader. Almost every kid who picked snacks was a seventh grader. The two groups weren't alike at all. Age had sneaked in and sorted them without anyone noticing.

That night she posted her tally in the chat. "I let people pick. Here's what happened." She sent the photo of the two crooked columns. "Now imagine the allergy study let everyone pick. The people choosing the new medicine might be different from the people choosing the old one, and you'd never know if the medicine worked or if the people were just different to start with."

Alix typed slowly, the bubble appearing and disappearing three times. "So the lab person wasn't being rude."

"No," Piper wrote. "They assign people to groups at random, so differences like age or health get spread evenly across both groups instead of piling up in one." She hit send, then added, "Random is the rudder. It steers the study straight."

Eloi's reply popped up: "Okay but in the allergy study, does everyone at least get snacks?"

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12.
story:
Gavin set his sleeping bag on the floor beside Mika's bed, next to a lamp shaped like a mushroom that glowed faintly even when switched off. "The plan," Mika announced, "is to stay awake until sunrise. Oceane stayed up until five at her cousin's house. She saw the sky turn pink." Gavin felt a stab of envy. He had never once seen the sky turn pink from the inside of a sleepover. He wanted this night to be the one he remembered.

Then he remembered the soccer game. Kickoff was at nine the next morning, and the coach had promised that anyone who looked sleepy would ride the bench. Gavin did some quick counting on his fingers. If the game started at nine, and he had to be up by seven thirty to eat and get there, then falling asleep at two would give him only five and a half hours. That seemed thin.

"Five and a half hours is nothing," he said. "Oceane's cousin is twelve, and even she can't run on that."

"So run on candy," Mika said, holding up a bag of sour worms. "It's voluntary, remember. Nobody's forcing you to stay up." But Gavin was already doing more counting, slower this time. His mother had read something out loud last month from a pamphlet at the dentist's office, something she'd made him repeat back. Children aged six to twelve needed nine to twelve hours of sleep a night. He had rolled his eyes at the time, because he was ten and the pamphlet was clearly meant for babies who were six. Now he added it up in reverse. Nine hours from seven thirty meant lights out by ten thirty. Twelve hours would mean falling asleep at seven thirty, which was impossible before a sleepover.

"Here's my test," he told Mika. "We stay up as late as we want, but I set an alarm experiment. If I fall asleep at midnight, I get seven and a half hours, under nine, and I'll be sluggish by the second half. If I knock out at ten, I get nine and a half, right inside the range. I want to see if the pamphlet is true. If I feel great, then the plan for the next sleepover is a ten o'clock lights out and nobody can argue."

Mika thought this was the most boring experiment ever invented, but he agreed to stay awake with Gavin until ten "for science." They ate sour worms, looked at the glowing fungus on the desk lamp, and whispered about the new kid at school until, somewhere past ten, both of them drifted off mid-sentence.

At seven the next morning, Gavin's phone buzzed. There was a text from the coach. The field was waterlogged. Game cancelled, enjoy your Saturday. Gavin stared at the screen, wide awake after nine hours of perfect sleep, with an entire free day stretching ahead and nothing to spend it on. He leaned over and shook Mika's shoulder. "Mika. Mika, wake up. The experiment's ruined and it's the best news I've ever had."

Katherine was staying at her grandmother's house for the week, and on Tuesday morning she found the old laptop in the study would not let her in. A sticky note beside it read "Ask Russell." That was strange, because Russell lived three streets over, but he had house-sat for Grandma last month and apparently changed things.

She called him, and he answered with a proud grin. "I made your grandma an exceptional password. Watch this." He held his phone up to the screen and typed, slowly, letter by letter: p@ssw0rd. "See? Nobody would ever guess that. It's got symbols and a number."

Katherine stared at it. Something about the word itched at her memory, and then the flashback arrived whole: last fall, Mr. Sánchez, who taught computers at the community center, had put a projector up in the library. He had shown a screen full of attempts ticking past, faster than anyone could read, and said only one sentence before the fire alarm went off. "Password-guessing programs try dictionary words, names, and common swaps like '@' for 'a' or '0' for 'o' early, so those swaps add little strength." The room had emptied in a rush of vapor from the science lab down the hall, and nobody had ever gone back to the talk.

"So it's like the program already knows about the @ and the zero," Katherine said now, half to Russell and half to herself.

"Knows about them?" Russell's grin wobbled. He had wanted all week for someone to call his password clever, and she could see it mattered to him.

"It tries them early. Like, first. Guessing isn't a person tapping keys. It's a program running through lists." She paused, then decided she could infer one more thing: if Russell had used this password for Grandma's laptop, he had probably used it for his own accounts too, because he was exactly the sort of person who found one good idea and stuck to it. "Russell. Did you use this same one for your email?"

The silence on the line lasted three full seconds.

"Okay," he said. "New plan. You make the password, and I'll make lunch. Deal?"

"Deal. Meet me at the kitchen table in ten minutes." She hung up, pulled the laptop toward her, and opened a blank document to start building something long, random, and truly hard to guess.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Squash plants grow separate male and female flowers, and only a female flower, which has a tiny fruit at its base, can grow into a squash after being pollinated.
story:
Easton had enrolled in the farm's junior grower program mostly so he could ride Mr. Krause's ancient tractor, but now, three weeks in, he cared more about the squash plant he'd been given. It sat in a sunny patch behind the barn, big green leaves, stems prickly as a hairbrush, and by late June it was covered in flowers. Orange ones, wide as his palm, opening every single morning.

"Fourteen flowers," he announced on Saturday, counting again to be sure. "That's fourteen squashes."

Landon, who had claimed the plant next to his, only had six flowers and looked glum about it. "You're going to bury me."

But a week later, Easton had zero squashes. The flowers opened, glowed like little lanterns, then folded up and dropped off, one by one, onto the dirt. Landon's plant, meanwhile, had two green marbles on it, fat and shiny, with flowers stuck on their ends like party hats.

"That's an illusion," Easton told Sami, pointing at his own plant. "It looks like a squash factory but it makes nothing." He crouched down and sniffed a bloom, sweet and faintly honeylike, then frowned. Something about the two plants had to be different. He checked the soil. Same. Water, same. Sun, same.

So he looked closer at the flowers themselves. On Landon's plant, two of the blooms weren't sitting on stems the way his were. They sat on tiny swollen knobs, like the flower had swallowed a green olive. He walked the row twice, checking every bloom, and found the pattern: only flowers with the little knob at the base had turned into squash. The plain ones, on plain stems, all fell off.

"Those knob ones are the girls," Sami said, peering over his shoulder. "My grandma calls them female flowers. The others are male. Only the girls make fruit."

Easton hunted through his plant and found, way down near the bottom, one single female flower hiding under a leaf, its baby squash no bigger than his thumbnail. One squash out of all those blooms. It felt like a joke the plant was playing on him.

The next morning he came back with a small paintbrush from the craft box, brushed it gently inside a male flower, then touched it to the female one, the way he'd seen bees do it without knowing why. He wrote the date on a durable metal plant tag, in pencil, and pressed it into the dirt beside her.

"Okay," he said to the little green thumb. "Your turn."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Jaxson arrived at Riverside Park with his basketball under one arm, hoping the pick-up game near the courts would crowd out the thing he kept replaying in his head. Greyson had skipped the sleepover. Not texted late, not shown up late, just skipped, after promising for two weeks. Jaxson had decided what that meant: Greyson was selfish. He'd been deciding it all morning, and a stubborn part of him didn't want to let it go, because being angry was easier than feeling replaced.

Imane was already at the courts, spinning a ball on her finger. "Greyson's not coming," she said, keeping her voice neutral, like she wasn't taking sides. "He texted the group chat. Something about his grandma."

"He could've told me." Jaxson's hands tightened on the ball, and the aluminum alloy rim above them seemed to hum in the wind, the whole court suddenly loud with everything unsaid.

"You assumed it's about you," Imane said. "Maybe think about what was going on with him, not just what kind of person he is." She tossed him the ball. "My sister calls that the fundamental attribution error, by the way. Blaming someone's character while ignoring their situation."

Jaxson stood there while the other kids argued over teams. A hidden cause, Imane had suggested. He couldn't see Greyson's grandma, or Greyson's house, or whatever had actually happened Friday night. He'd built a whole story about Greyson's character out of one missing evening, the way people build a bridge out of one plank. It wasn't proof of anything. It was just the easiest story, and the easiest story was usually wrong.

That night he read the message three times before he could sit still enough to answer. "I get it now," he typed. "Meet at the park tomorrow? I'll bring the ball."

Greyson was waiting by the swings when Jaxson rode up the next morning, his bike's frame still dull with rain. "She fell in the kitchen Friday night," Greyson said, scuffing gravel with his shoe. "I was at the hospital until two in the morning. I kept meaning to text, but my phone was dead and my head was, like, nowhere."

"I thought you just ditched me," Jaxson admitted. "That was dumb."

"Pretty dumb." Greyson almost smiled. "Is she okay?"

"Broke her wrist. She's home. She kept asking if you were okay, because apparently I looked wrecked."

They walked to the courts, and Jaxson noticed Greyson's shots kept falling short, his shoulders sagging after each one. So Jaxson started feeding him easy passes, the kind you give someone who needs to make one basket before anything inside them settles. It would have hindered the game to slow down like that, and the other kids groaned, but Jaxson kept doing it anyway.

Greyson sank a shot from the corner, finally, and turned with his arms up. "Six to two," he called, "and I'm coming back."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

story:
The meatloaf was halfway to Hailey's mouth when her dad said it again. "This is the best chili I've ever made." He said it every time, even the batch with the burnt bottom, even the batch the dog wouldn't touch. Hailey put her fork down. "How do you know it's the best? Did you taste all the other batches side by side?" Her mother slid a pharmacy bag off the table, shook out her prescription, and set the bottle where Hailey could read the label. "You can't argue with a man and his chili," her mother said. But Hailey was already looking at the label, at the plain words on it: take one tablet twice daily. That, she thought, you could check. You could count the pills. You could call the pharmacy. "Best" you couldn't check. "Best" was just her dad's opinion wearing a crown.

She had a bet riding on this. Ansh had sworn that the review he read online proved Sparkle Blast was "the best toothpaste ever," and whoever lost the argument had to carry the other one's backpack for a week. After dinner Hailey grabbed her phone, found the review, and started highlighting words: best, worst, beautiful, boring, should. Every sentence with one of those words fell apart the moment she asked, could I check this? "Whitens teeth in seven days" could be tested. "Should be in every bathroom" could not. She typed fast, eager to refute Ansh before he could gloat, and stopped with her thumb over send.

Because at the bottom of the page, in tiny gray letters, she found the sentence that changed everything: the reviewer had been paid by the toothpaste company. All those judgment words, all that "best ever," suddenly seemed less like a person's honest opinion and more like a fishing lure. Ansh's whole source was plausible-looking and hollow, a fake rock with something wiggling underneath.

At school the next morning, she slid her phone across the lab table before Ansh could even sit down. He read it, groaned, and stared at the ceiling. "So I'm carrying your backpack." "Doubletime," Hailey said, and slung both straps over his shoulders herself.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: Scratch, a block-based programming language, was developed at the MIT Media Lab and first released in 2007.
story:
The first thing Asher noticed about Esteban's basement was the cold, so Esteban's dad had covered part of the floor with old carpet scraps to insulate it, and they sat cross-legged on that square while the laptop booted up. On the screen, an orange cat waited in a white box.

"Okay," Esteban said. "You said the score is broken. Show me."

Asher clicked the green flag. In his game, the cat had to catch falling apples, and every apple touched was supposed to add one point. But the score jumped from zero to forty-seven in a single second, then to a hundred, then higher, spinning like a slot machine even though the cat wasn't touching anything. Last Saturday he had stared at the same problem for an hour, closed the laptop, and told himself he was not a coder. He thought about that now, sitting in the cold basement, and decided an hour wasn't enough. He was going to give it two.

Clementine leaned in from the beanbag chair. "It's counting when it shouldn't. Something invisible is happening."

"Exactly," Asher said. "So the problem is inside the code, not on the screen. I can't see it, but it follows a rule. I just have to find the rule." He had an idea. What if the score was adding one point every split second, forever, because he had dragged the "change score by 1" block inside the forever loop by mistake? The loop would run and run whether the cat touched an apple or not. To test it, he pulled that block out of the loop and dropped it inside an if-then block, the one that checked "touching apple." He set the if-then back inside the forever loop and clicked the flag.

The score sat still at zero. The cat caught an apple. One. Another apple. Two. Asher punched the air so hard he knocked over Esteban's half-full cup, and they all dove to save the keyboard before the juice could reach it.

"You found the hidden rule," Esteban said, toweling the desk. "The loop was the culprit."

"I only found it because it kept doing the same wrong thing over and over," Asher said. "The pattern gave it away."

Upstairs, a door slammed, and the old copper pipe running along the ceiling, a perfect conductor of every sound in the house, carried the noise down loud as a drum. "That's my grandma leaving," Esteban said. "Wait, you never answered her letter."

Asher pulled the folded page from his backpack. His eccentric grandmother, who still wrote actual letters and mailed them with stamps, had asked what he was doing all weekend. He'd written back that he was coding, and she had replied in purple ink: "Coding? With a keyboard full of zeros and ones, like your uncle did? You are eleven!"

He borrowed Esteban's pen and wrote at the bottom of her letter: "No keyboard at all, Grandma. I snap blocks together like LEGO. The program is called Scratch. It was developed at the MIT Media Lab and first released in 2007, before I was even born. Next time you visit, I'll teach you."

He read it over, grinned, and said, "She's going to try to drag the blocks with her finger on the screen, isn't she?"

"Definitely," said Clementine. "Now click the flag again. I want to beat your high score."

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Reframing means restating an insult in neutral words, turning "She's so selfish" into "You want a fairer share," so the conversation can keep moving.
story:
The bus smelled like wet jackets and floor cleaner, and Edouard had barely sat down before the shouting started two rows back. Hunter was holding his basketball with both arms like someone might steal it. "Ronan never passes. He's so selfish, he thinks the whole game is about him."

Ronan's ears went red. "Take that back."

Edouard turned around in his seat. He had watched these two argue before, and it always ended the same way: Hunter yelled an insult, Ronan yelled it back louder, and neither one spoke to the other for a week. A chronic problem, his mother would call it, the kind that keeps coming back no matter how many times you patch it up. The bus lurched around a corner, and Hunter slid into the aisle, still gripping the ball.

"Wait," Edouard said, standing up. "Before you say anything back, Ronan. Let me try something."

Ronan crossed his arms. "Why? You're just going to take Hunter's side."

"I'm not taking anyone's side." Edouard thought fast. Last month he had watched a video about mediators, the people who step between two sides, and one part had stuck with him. The trick wasn't to stop the argument. It was to change what got repeated. He took a breath. "Hunter, you said Ronan is so selfish. What I heard is that you want a fairer share of the ball."

Hunter blinked. "That's not what I said."

"That's what it means, though," Edouard said. "You want a fairer share."

The bus rumbled over a pothole. Ronan uncrossed his arms slowly. "I didn't know it looked like that from your side," he said to Hunter. "I thought I was taking the shots I was supposed to take. Coach says I'm the best at layups."

"You are the best at layups," Hunter admitted. "But you take twenty shots a game and I take like four."

"So say that next time," Ronan said. "Say you want a fairer share, not that I'm selfish."

"That's called reframing," Edouard said. "Restating the mean version in neutral words so the conversation keeps moving."

Hunter looked at him. "Where'd you acquire that trick, a monk school?"

Edouard laughed. "The internet. You want to learn the other components? There's a whole video."

Ronan scooted over to make room on his seat. "Show us at lunch. But no talking during the good part of the video, or you're off the case." He patted the empty spot, and Edouard sat down between them as the bus hissed to a stop.

story:

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score

fact: Scratch is named after DJ scratching, where a record is moved back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds.
story:
Henry's sneaker bounced against the leg of Theron's basement couch, because there was no way he could sit still with a half-finished game glowing on the screen. The cat sprite was supposed to gain a point every time it caught the bouncing donut, but the score stayed stuck at zero no matter what he did.

"You put the if-then inside the wrong loop," Theron said, leaning over his shoulder. "The forever block has to wrap around it, or the game only checks once."

"That's it?" Henry dragged the forever block around the if-then, snapped it in place, and hit the green flag. The donut dropped, the cat leapt, and the number in the corner jumped from 0 to 1. Henry let out a whoot loud enough to provoke a thump on the ceiling from Theron's dad upstairs, which made both of them laugh and then clamp their hands over their mouths.

The real problem was the deadline. Ms. Lavoie had announced a coding showcase on Friday, and Henry wanted sound in his game, real sound, not the meow that came with the cat. Theron's older cousin had left a turntable down here, a dusty one with a slipmat and a record still on it, and Waylon was already spinning the record backward with his fingertip.

"Careful," Theron said, but Waylon just grinned.

"You know why they call it Scratch, right?" Waylon said. "It's named after DJ scratching, moving a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Henry stared at the screen, then at the record, then at the screen again. He could mix sounds and code in the same game. That was the whole point of the name. His fingers flew across the keyboard, recording Waylon scratching a short wah-wah sound, saving it, dropping it into a "play sound" block inside the if-then. Now every donut catch would make the remix noise.

The first test failed. The sound played on every frame because Henry had put the play block before the if-then instead of inside it, so it turned into a chronic stutter, wah-wah-wah-wah, until he hit stop. His ears rang. Waylon covered his head with a couch cushion.

"Inside," Theron said. "Inside the if-then."

Henry dragged the block in, nested it snug, and ran it again. The donut fell, the cat caught it, the score ticked to 1, and one clean wah rang out through the basement. He saved the file twice, because guilt over last month's lost homework project still haunted him, and he was not losing this.

"Friday," Waylon said, spinning the record one more time. "Ms. Lavoie is going to freak."

Henry hit the green flag and watched the score climb.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why

story:
"Phones in the basket," said Oceane's mother, holding out a wooden bowl like she was collecting treasure. "Sunset's in ten minutes." Camille stared at her phone, then at the window, where the sky over the synagogue across the street was turning orange. Then she lit two candles, cupped her hands over the flame, and closed her eyes, and Camille suddenly felt like she was watching something private through a window.

Camille handed over her phone slowly, as if the basket might bite. "When do I get it back?" she asked. "Tomorrow night," Oceane's father said, smiling. "After it's fully dark on Saturday." Twenty-four hours. Camille's mind went straight to the math: sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday, the whole stretch of a day bounded by the sky instead of a clock. Nobody had told her a day could have soft edges. She thought of her grandmother, who turned off her own phone every Sunday and grew tomatoes in her fertile little garden patch, humming. Camille had always figured that was just a grandma thing. Now she wondered if it was a choice you could make on purpose, like choosing to modify the airplane's bent pin so the propeller spun the right way.

They walked to the synagogue for the evening service. Inside, the singing rose and fell, and a boy named Drew, who had followed them because his dog had followed them, whispered, "Do they have snacks at this thing?" Someone behind them laughed so hard she dropped her prayer book, which made Drew look extremely pleased with himself. Camille found she was humming along before she knew the tune.

The next afternoon, phoneless and slightly bored, Camille and Oceane and Drew rebuilt the airplane on the synagogue's front steps.
